details:
**Liberty Leading the People**
Delacroix's most famous painting, commemorating the July Revolution of 1830 that toppled King Charles X. A bare-breasted, barefoot woman personifying Liberty (Marianne), in a Phrygian cap and yellow dress, strides over a pile of corpses holding the French tricolor in one hand and a bayoneted musket in the other. She is flanked by a man in a top hat holding a musket and a boy brandishing two pistols, while a half-clothed corpse in the foreground wears a single blue sock. The towers of Notre-Dame appear in the smoky background, and the figures' hats indicate their different social classes.

**The Death of Sardanapalus**
An 1827 painting inspired by Lord Byron's play Sardanapalus. The last king of Assyria reclines indifferently on a huge red bed decorated with golden elephant heads while his servants slaughter his concubines and horses before his own impending suicide. A man in a turban stabs a nude woman in the foreground and another tries to kill a white horse; one woman beside an elephant head is the only figure looking at the viewer.

**The Massacre at Chios**
An 1824 painting of the slaughter of Greek civilians on the island of Chios by Ottoman troops in 1822, during the Greek War of Independence. An Ottoman soldier on a rearing horse at right has a nude Greek woman tied to his horse as he draws his saber, while in the foreground a baby reaches for the breast of its dead mother and an old woman stares blankly. Delacroix reportedly repainted parts of it more vividly after seeing John Constable's The Hay Wain.

**The Barque of Dante**
Delacroix's 1822 Salon debut, depicting a scene from Dante's Inferno. Dante and his guide, the Roman poet Virgil, are rowed across the River Styx by Phlegyas as the City of Dis smokes in the background, while tormented damned souls cling to the boat and one bites at the wood. It was heavily influenced by Théodore Géricault's The Raft of the Medusa; works by the two artists dominate Room 77 of the Louvre's Denon wing.

**The Women of Algiers**
An 1834 painting (Women of Algiers in Their Apartment) based on Delacroix's 1832 trip to North Africa. Three women sit on rugs around a hookah in a harem interior while a Black servant turns and walks away at left. Pablo Picasso painted a famous series of variations on it.

**Ovid Among the Scythians**
A painting showing the Roman poet Ovid in exile at Tomis on the Black Sea, surrounded by curious barbarian Scythians. In the foreground a man milks a mare, a practice the poet finds strange, while another offers him food. It relates to Delacroix's decoration of the library ceiling of the Palais Bourbon, which includes an Ovid scene.

**Greece on the Ruins of Missolonghi**
An 1826 allegorical painting (also called Greece Expiring on the Ruins of Missolonghi) commemorating the Ottoman siege of the Greek town of Missolonghi, where Byron died. A woman in white, personifying Greece, kneels on a slanted slab of rubble with her arms outstretched and palms open, a hand protruding from the debris beneath her, while a turbaned Ottoman soldier stands in the background.

**The Entry of the Crusaders into Constantinople**
An 1840 painting of the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople in 1204. Baldwin of Flanders, who became the first Latin Emperor of Constantinople, and his knights on horseback look down at the pleading inhabitants of the burning city.

**Tiger Hunt and Lion Hunt**
Delacroix painted many violent animal-hunt scenes, influenced by the hunt paintings of Peter Paul Rubens, in which mounted hunters spear or fight big cats. He also painted quieter animal scenes such as a Young Tiger Playing with Its Mother.

**Still Life with Lobsters**
A still life showing lobsters on a table alongside hunting game such as a hare and birds and hunting rifles, set before a landscape background.

**Portrait of Chopin and George Sand**
A double portrait of the composer Frédéric Chopin and his lover, the novelist George Sand, later cut into two separate canvases. Delacroix was a close friend of Chopin and served as a pallbearer at his funeral; he also painted a portrait of the violinist Niccolò Paganini.

**Murals at Saint-Sulpice**
Delacroix's final major project, murals for the Chapel of the Holy Angels in the Paris church of Saint-Sulpice, completed in 1861. They include Heliodorus Driven from the Temple and Jacob Wrestling with the Angel.

**Horse Frightened by a Storm**
A watercolor in which a white horse twists its neck backwards in fear as a bolt of lightning strikes in the upper left corner. Horses were a recurring subject for Delacroix.

**The Orphan Girl at the Cemetery**
A study of a young girl in a graveyard looking upward with tearful, frightened eyes, often considered a preparatory study for a figure in The Massacre at Chios.
